Massacre of Glencoe. It occurred on February 13, 1692, in the Scottish Highlands, when government soldiers, billeted among the Macdonald clan of Glencoe, rose at dawn and systematically killed approximately 30 to 40 clan members—men, women, and children. The soldiers had been ostensibly quartered peacefully, but the massacre was ordered by Scottish government officials and sanctioned by King William II, ostensibly as punishment for the Macdonalds' late submission after the failed Jacobite Rising of 1690. The event became a symbol of Highland oppression, the betrayal of hospitality, and government tyranny, and it accelerated the decline of the traditional clan system in Scotland.

The Jacobite Rising of 1690 had failed, and government forces were consolidating control over the Highlands, where clans remained semi-autonomous. A royal proclamation demanded all clan chiefs submit by January 1, 1692. Those who complied would receive pardons and protection, and those who resisted would face military suppression. The Macdonald of Glencoe, the elderly clan chief, was traveling to submit when weather delayed him, and his late submission was technically in violation of the deadline.

Government troops, under the command of Robert Campbell of Glen Lyon, were quartered in Glencoe allegedly to collect taxes or conduct routine garrison duties. On the morning of February 13, soldiers rose and attacked the Macdonald clanspeople. Some were killed in their beds, others shot as they fled. Approximately 30 to 40 were killed, though some sources cite higher numbers. Others escaped into the winter mountains, and the violence lasted only hours but was systematic.

The massacre violated Highland customs of hospitality and protection. Soldiers had been guests in Macdonald homes and were fed by families they then murdered. Government orders explicitly authorized killing women and children, with the explicit intent to eliminate the clan as a political entity. Robert Campbell, though sympathetic to the Macdonalds, obeyed his orders and reported back to Scottish officials that the action had been completed.

News of the massacre spread rapidly and shocked even the harshly administered Scottish Highlands. Inquiry revealed government authorization at the highest levels. A parliamentary investigation in 1695 concluded that government ministers had acted illegally and tyrannically, but no prosecutions occurred. Those responsible faced only political disgrace. Survivors and the Macdonald clan were forever marked as victims of government treachery, and the massacre became a trauma in Highland memory.

Glencoe accelerated the decline of the clan system. Clanspeople increasingly doubted the government's good faith and relied less on traditional leadership. The massacre became a symbol of Highland oppression, reinforcing anti-government sentiment that would fuel the Jacobite cause for decades. The event's infamy stemmed not from its scale but from its flagrant violation of social norms and its explicit targeting of a whole people. For the Macdonalds and wider Highland culture, Glencoe became a foundational trauma that shaped identity and politics for centuries, accelerating the militarization of the Highlands as the government deployed soldiers to suppress potential rebellions.
